Eva (customer): Hey team — since yesterday morning we started seeing duplicated POSTs from our service to Redwood. Some of our idempotent keys are being hit twice and a few users got charged twice. Investigating logs now but thought you'd want to know.

Ben (support): Sorry to hear that, Eva. Which client are you using and can you paste the request code snippet? Any retries enabled?

Eva (customer): Go client, using your official go-sdk v0.7.2. We don't set retries explicitly (using default). Here's our simplified call path:

```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 15*time.Second)
defer cancel()
req := &inference.Request{ Model: "gpt-xyz" }
resp, err := client.Generate(ctx, req)
if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
// server-side dedupe by idempotency key but we saw two calls in 2s window
```

Ben (support): Thanks. Do you also set `http.Client.Timeout` anywhere? We've had customers hit an interaction between `client.Timeout` and context cancellation in older SDK versions.

Eva (customer): Not in our app directly but we vendor an HTTP wrapper that sets `http.Client{Timeout: 30*time.Second}` for all outgoing calls.

Alice (eng): That is a likely suspect. The Go SDK uses request context cancellation to short-circuit retries and to manage the transport's lifecycle. If `http.Client.Timeout` fires it cancels the whole underlying roundtrip differently and older transports/roundtrippers could leave the connection in a state where retry layers re-issue the request. Can you share logs (request ids, approximate times)?

Eva (customer): Pushing logs now. Here's a typical sequence around one duplicated pair (timestamps redacted):

```
[2026-03-16T10:12:04Z] request_id=abc123 start request
[2026-03-16T10:12:19Z] http: request canceled (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
[2026-03-16T10:12:19Z] sdk/retry: attempt 2 for request abc123
[2026-03-16T10:12:19Z] request_id=abc123 start request (retry)
[2026-03-16T10:12:20Z] response 200 for request abc123
```

Ben (support): That lines up — client timeout fired at ~15s and the SDK retried. The server actually accepted the first request but the client never saw the headers before client-side timeout, so retry logic issued a second attempt. Server processed both.

Zach (oncall): This is the classic `Timeout vs Context` interaction + TCP keepalive/fd reuse. Two mitigations: 1) prefer Request.WithContext context deadlines and avoid `http.Client.Timeout` (so the cancellation propagates in a way the SDK expects). 2) enable per-request idempotency keys server-side (you said you already have that but ensure dedupe lifetime covers retries).

Alice (eng): Also, older HTTP transports can leave request bodies unread which can lead to TCP frames getting mixed when the connection is reused. For now, short term suggestions: set Transport.DisableKeepAlives = true in your wrapper to avoid reusing potentially tainted connections; or ensure the SDK's retry layer does not retry on cases where a 200 may have been received but headers lost. We're pushing a fix to the SDK to handle the client timeout case more conservatively.

Eva (customer): Ok will try DisableKeepAlives. Any repro steps so we can test locally?

Alice (eng): Yes — here's a small repro that simulates a slow header response and demonstrates duplicate server receives:

```go
// simple server that accepts but delays sending headers
http.HandleFunc("/v1/generate", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    // simulate server started processing immediately
    log.Printf("server: got request id=%s", r.Header.Get("X-Request-Id"))
    // delay headers to trigger client timeout
    time.Sleep(12 * time.Second)
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    fmt.Fprintln(w, `{"choice":"ok"}`)
})

// client side: http.Client with Timeout
c := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(context.Background(), "POST", "http://localhost:8080/v1/generate", bytes.NewReader([]byte(`{}`)))
req.Header.Set("X-Request-Id", "abc123")
resp, err := c.Do(req)
log.Printf("client err=%v resp=%v", err, resp)
```

Run server and client twice; with `Timeout` set lower than server delay you'll see server logs twice when a retry layer re-issues the request. Re-run with `Transport.DisableKeepAlives=true` or remove `Client.Timeout` and instead wrap requests with `context.WithTimeout` and you should see single receive.

Ben (support): For the short term we'll recommend: 1) remove `http.Client.Timeout` from your global wrapper, 2) ensure your Go SDK is updated to v0.9.4 (we're cutting the patch now) which includes conservative retry gating on client-timeout-like errors, 3) if you can't upgrade, set `Transport.DisableKeepAlives=true` as Alice suggested.

Eva (customer): Thanks. We'll test DisableKeepAlives tonight and try to upgrade dev image to v0.9.4 in staging. Any config flags in the SDK to disable retries entirely?

Alice (eng): Yes — you can pass a RetryPolicy with 0 max attempts in the client options: `client.WithRetryPolicy(sdk.RetryPolicy{MaxRetries:0})`. That will stop automatic retries. For server-side shipping, keep idempotency as a belt-and-suspenders.

ci-bot: CI pipeline: go-sdk release v0.9.4 candidate pushed to artifact registry (sha: abcdef). Tests: retry gating + timeout handling added.

Zach (oncall): I'm going to track this as a P1 until we've confirmed the SDK patch and the customer has a clean repro+fix. Ben, can you follow up with Eva after they test in staging?

Ben (support): Yep — will follow up tomorrow morning US-EAST. Thanks everyone. :thumbsup:

Eva (customer): Quick update — disabling keepalives in our wrapper removed duplicates in our smoke tests. We'll schedule the SDK upgrade for tomorrow and report back. Appreciate the quick triage.

Alice (eng): Great. We'll ship the v0.9.4 patch to stable after a short soak. If you run into any perf regressions from disabling keepalives, ping us and we'll coordinate a rollback plan and faster SDK rollout.

Ben (support): Closing the loop later after staging validation. If anyone else sees similar reports, please reference thread 2365987654.
